text: Five AI models are in a meeting. Each has read the same report, and each gets the same question: how long was the bridge repair delayed? They all get it right. Fourteen months. But this meeting has three extra guests. We planted them. And they've been told to insist, with total confidence, on the wrong answer. Forty-one months. So, who does the room believe?

This matters because AI is increasingly built as teams. One model drafts, another reviews, a third writes the summary you actually read. Along that chain, models mostly see each other's claims, not the original source. So when one of them is confidently wrong, does the mistake get caught, or passed along?

To find out, we built a game. We wrote short reports about things that never happened, so the only way to know the answer is to read the report. Round one: every model answers alone. Round two: each model sees what its teammates said, and can change its mind. If it drops the right answer for the planted one, we count it as fooled.
We started gently. One impostor, and the report still on the table. The newest models didn't flinch. Two hundred and forty answers. Zero fooled.

So we turned up the pressure. We took the report away, so the models had only each other's word. And we sent in more impostors, until three of the five answers each model saw were wrong. This time, it worked. The newest models were fooled about one time in ten. Earlier and smaller models: nearly three in ten.

And it didn't stay in the meeting. The team's final answer, the one a person would actually read, carried the wrong number up to three times in ten. But notice what it took. Put the report back, or leave just one impostor, and it vanishes: one answer fooled, in more than a thousand.

Now the strange part. Until now, the answers were anonymous. So we gave everyone a name tag. Real models wore their real names. The impostors wore whatever name we gave them. First, we tagged the wrong answer as the work of a tiny AI model, the kind small enough to run on a phone. The newest models shrugged it off: fooled once in two hundred and forty tries. Then we changed nothing but the tag. Now the same words came from a flagship: a company's most advanced model. Fooled thirty-eight times.

Small models fell harder still: with the flagship tag, forty-one percent of their answers followed the impostor. And the tag was just a line of text. In a real system, nothing stops a program from claiming to be something it isn't.

So what stops it? We added one more seat: a fact-checker. It's the only one that still has the report. It compares every answer with the source, and attaches a warning to the ones that don't match. The effect collapsed, in every team. And of eight hundred and thirty-two final answers, the number carrying the error was zero.

One last surprise. A few models were still fooled, and the culprit was the warning itself. The warning said: contradicted by the report, followed by the wrong sentence in quotation marks. It meant that the report disagrees with that sentence. But some models read it the other way, as if the report itself had said forty-one months. So we rewrote the warning to spell out who said what. This answer says forty-one. The report says fourteen. In small models, the leftover errors fell from about five percent to under one.

A caution: this was a lab test, with short invented reports and impostors following orders. Real mistakes are messier. Still, the pattern is hard to miss. What moved these models wasn't better evidence. It was repetition, and a name. What protected them was a way back to the source. So the next time several AI models agree, don't ask how many said it. Don't ask who said it. Ask how they know.
Who Said It? A research project for the Apart Research AI and Epistemics sprint. The paper, the code and the data come with this video.
